vo.text: In 1415, a small, sick, soaking wet English army was about to face one of the biggest armies in France. Spoiler: the mud picked a side.
King Henry the Fifth of England had invaded France to claim its crown. He captured a port town. And then a lot of his army got sick. Very, very sick. Let's just say the bushes were busy.
So Henry decided to march to Calais, an English town on the French coast, and go home. The French army blocked the road.
On the twenty-fifth of October, the two armies faced each other across a freshly ploughed field, with thick woods on both sides.
Henry had maybe eight thousand men. Most of them were archers with longbows. The French had far more, and many were knights in heavy armour.
It had rained all night. The field was now deep, sticky mud.
The English archers hammered sharp wooden stakes into the ground in front of them. Then Henry moved his whole army forward. Close enough to shoot.
Thousands of arrows went up. And came down on the French.
French knights on horseback charged. But the mud slowed them, and the stakes stopped them. Their horses turned around and galloped back into their own side.
Then the French soldiers advanced on foot. Wearing armour. Through mud. Up to their knees.
The woods squeezed them into a narrow space. They were packed so tightly they could barely swing a weapon.
By the time they reached the English line, they were exhausted. And the English archers dropped their bows, grabbed hammers and axes, and joined in.
The French lines behind kept pushing into the ones in front. Chaos.
Within a few hours, it was over. Thousands of French soldiers were killed or captured, including many of the greatest lords in France. The English lost a few hundred.
Almost two hundred years later, Shakespeare turned the battle into a famous play. We few. We happy few.
Henry went on to marry the French king's daughter, and was named heir to France. And French knights learned a lesson: always check the weather.
